units: the job began as an ordinary check

the roofing specialist flagged a crack hidden under the coating

text: The site foreman says the whole thing started out as an ordinary check, nothing more. He had climbed the scaffolding to look at the gable end when he noticed a roof tile working loose. The roofer with him caught more than that: a thin crack ran beneath the render, and from the yard below almost nobody would have picked it out. They called the owner, who refused to let anyone patch anything until a full survey had been done. The mason brought in later scraped the surface back and found the binder crumbling and soft, washed out by the weather. The timber frame, he says, had come through untouched. The crew then packed the wall with a mix of sand and lime, and once that had set they laid the covering back in place. The owner now says the front wall will hold without anyone watching over it.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the exhaustion of the nearby deposits forced the builders to change material

the walls grew thinner

a lime based coating served as breathable protection
the craftsmen had to learn to judge a firing instead of a quarried block
the old buildings still keep the mark of that change
text: When the quarries near the building sites ran dry, the men who raised walls had to think again. Stone grew scarce, and brick took its place, since it was lighter to lift and could be fired in kilns a short walk from the work itself. The change reached all the way into the shape of the buildings themselves. Walls grew thinner. Openings widened. The vault gave way to flat ceilings carried on beams. Brick, though, drank water badly, so a lime coating went over it, one that let damp escape rather than trapping it. The trade shifted too. A mason no longer read the grain of a quarried block; he learned to judge a firing by its color and its ring. Out of that shift came a way of building that rose faster and cost less, yet flinched at every long rain. The oldest walls still standing carry the mark of it.

units: the breaking of a poured floor almost always has a traceable origin
an uneven settling of the support unbalances the spread of the load
water working in makes the inner metal bars swell
that swelling widens the gap
the change is followed with a measuring device fixed on the surface
a gap that stops moving is treated at the surface
the treatment means opening the gap at an angle then filling it with a hardening product
a gap that keeps opening reveals a problem in the ground
the ground is then stabilized by injecting a product under the footings
text: A poured slab hardly ever splits without a reason you can trace. The ground under it settles unevenly, one side drops, and the load stops spreading the way it should. A gap opens, hair thin at first, then wider as water works in and swells the steel bars buried in the concrete. Anyone assessing the damage starts by tracking that gap: a gauge is glued across it and read at set intervals. If the reading holds steady, the repair stays shallow. You cut the crack open at an angle, clear the dust out, and pour in a resin that hardens cold. If the gap keeps growing, the fault lies in the ground rather than the slab, and a binder has to be injected beneath the footing to even the bearing out. Skip that step, and you will go on dressing the same wound forever while the soil keeps giving way beneath the patch.

units: a craftsman took charge of restoring an old farm building

the recent part showed breaks in several places
the cause of the trouble was not the age of the material but the pairing of two techniques
the craftsman advised taking down and rebuilding the recent part with a compatible binder
the owner ended up accepting the cost
text: The craftsman who agreed to restore the old farm building took the work on out of plain curiosity, and little else. On his first walk through it he found two ways of building stacked one above the other inside a single wall. Down below, earlier hands had set uneven stones in a fat, yielding mortar that still gave a little under the thumb. Above, added long afterward, sat hard blocks bedded in gray cement. The lower courses had shifted with the ground and taken no harm; the upper work had torn open in several places. What had failed, he concluded, was not the older material but the pairing of two techniques that answered to opposite logics. He advised taking the later section down and raising it again in a mortar close to the original. The owner balked at what that would cost, and in the end agreed to it.

units: you first gather the tools you need including a one wheeled carrier and a mason blade

it goes on in three successive coats
each coat has its own job: to grip, to fill, to level
a coat must dry away from any draft before the next one
the tools are cleaned straight after use
the binder is kept in a dry place
text: Before you set about rendering an old wall, put your kit together on the ground: a wheelbarrow, a bucket, a wide trowel, a float, and a sieve. Then get the wall ready. Rake out the crumbling patches, brush every trace of dust away, and damp the surface down without soaking it. Mixing comes next. Tip the sand into the barrow, work the lime in a little at a time, add water, and turn it until the paste clings to the blade instead of sliding off. Lay it on in three passes. The first grips the wall, the second fills the hollows, the third brings everything level. Let each coat dry right through, out of the draft, before you start the one above it. Finish by looking after the kit. Rinse the tools right away, empty the barrow, shut the binder in a dry store, and throw a cover over the sand heap.

text: The week got off to a rough start over on the site in the old quarter. The crew showed up to find the scaffolding leaning sideways, since one windy night had been enough to shove it out of true. Down the whole thing came, two full working days of it, and not one of them grumbled. Next morning, clearing out the loft, an apprentice came across a sealed hatch tucked under the rafters. People around here had heard talk of it for years and never really bought it. The architect came over, called a halt to the demolition, and just like that the job turned into a rescue. Since then, folks drift by at the end of the day for a look down the dark hole they reopened. The boss just grins about the whole business. He meant to hand the place over fast; now he knows it will be late, and it hardly bothers him.

units: the outside of the building gives an impression of good condition

that paint blistered quickly

text: Seen from the yard, the house looks perfectly sound. Pale front wall, straight gable, shutters all in line, and a visitor would walk in without a second thought. The inside tells quite another story. The floor under the roof space has begun to hump, because a split gutter has been emptying itself against the wall season after season. Damp has crept into the timbers, lifted the render off in flakes, and left a brown ring that grows a little wider with every downpour. Lower down, the hallway slab rings hollow: the sand it once rested on has washed out from underneath. The owners painted over the stain first, hoping to bury it. The paint blistered before the next winter was out, showing a wall soaked right through. The survey is blunt about it: start at the roof, or whatever you mend below will rot again.

units: the writer finds the spread of smooth front walls worrying
a cement based coating stops the wall from letting damp out
the trapped water ends up breaking the stone from within
the writer holds that a sealed surface was mistaken for a protected one
he proposes using binders that let vapor through
he advises keeping cement for the buried parts
he invites us to accept the visible aging of a wall
he calls for training craftsmen to examine old building work
a properly coated wall lasts several generations with light upkeep
text: Street after street is going over to smooth front walls that age badly, and the drift ought to worry us more than it does. A wall skinned in cement has stopped breathing. It holds water against the stone, and in time the stone bursts from within. We mistook a sealed surface for a protected one. The cure asks for no brilliance at all. Go back to binders that let vapor pass, keep cement for what sits below ground, and let a wall weather instead of demanding that it stay untouched. Craftsmen should be taught again how to read old masonry, a slow discipline that the rush of modern building has all but rubbed out. A wall coated the right way lasts generations on nothing more than an occasional wash of lime. We would rather keep redoing every so often what earlier hands managed to get right the first time.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)

text: The roofer who runs the site learned her trade from an old hand who never drew a single line. She likes to set the two schools of work against each other. He laid tile by eye, walked the pitch to correct it, and told whether a roof was tight by the sound rain made on it. She measures first, notes the angles, and works the layout out on paper before she climbs. He went up and down all day with the barrow; she makes up her loads on the ground and carries them once. On one point, though, she grants him the advantage. He could feel a tired frame flex under his boots, and no set of readings will give you that. So she kept one habit of his: walk the whole roof over before laying a hand on any of it. Her jobs now run shorter than they did in her early years, without losing anything in strength.

units: the verdict on this conversion falls into three parts

text: This conversion calls for a divided verdict, one that falls readily into three parts. The first is structure. The carpenters kept the original trusses and doubled them so quietly that the eye passes over the work, and the span still reads clean from one end of the hall to the other. The second is the finishing, and here the praise thins out. The render chosen is too hard, and it has already cracked where the loads come down, while the slab, poured in one unbroken sheet, takes no account of a ground that moves. The third part concerns use. The place is a pleasure to walk through, the way in and out stays obvious, and the sound has been tamed without a single panel on show. One regret remains: the floor under the roof is kept for staff alone, which denies visitors the finest view of the vault.
